claims.text: Local chemical complexity in Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni-derived concentrated alloys causes spatial variation in dislocation slip activation energy.
Variation in dislocation slip activation energy is the dominant mechanism governing strength and deformation in these alloys.
Spatially varying slip activation produces locally heterogeneous slip during compression.
Locally heterogeneous slip governs the overall mechanical response.
Thermal activation plays a significant role from ambient to moderately elevated temperatures.
Local dislocation structures and slip-band formations mediate the effect of local chemical fluctuations on slip activation energy.
Local chemical complexity causes variations in atomic displacements.
Variations in atomic displacements modify the energy barriers for dislocation slip.
Increasing strain rate makes the effects of locally modified slip activation energies more pronounced.
The proposed response is distinct from one governed solely by grain-boundary effects.
Higher strain rates will increase the apparent slip activation energy.
The predicted activation-energy change will be observable through a change in strain-rate sensitivity.
Higher-rate compression will produce more localized slip bands than lower-rate compression.
Lower-rate compression will produce a more uniform dislocation distribution.
Models that omit chemical complexity predict a homogeneous distribution of slip activation energies.
A traditional interpretation attributes strength and deformation primarily to grain-boundary strengthening and uniformly distributed slip barriers.
The qualitative effect of local chemical complexity on slip activation is supported by strain-rate-jump experiments.
The qualitative effect of local chemical complexity on slip activation is supported by DFT predictions.

contradictions.description: The proposed specimens are single crystals, while the stated baseline emphasizes grain-boundary strengthening. This makes the grain-boundary baseline poorly matched to the tested material state and prevents a direct controlled comparison of the rival mechanisms.
